Running a Win-Loss Programme

The Commercial SystemPart 25

By lowob · 16 October 2026 · 9-minute read · Revenue

A win-loss programme is a standing process that asks buyers why they chose as they did, codes the answers against a fixed frame, and routes each recurring theme to someone who must decide what to change. The one-off study is common; the programme is rare. Gartner analyst Todd Berkowitz has argued that no more than a third of sales organisations run win-loss with rigour, and win-loss vendor Clozd reports that buyer and seller loss reasons align only 15% of the time. The fix is less about better interviews than about what happens after them: a sampling rule, a neutral interviewer, and a decision record for every finding.

Most firms with more than a handful of sellers have run a win-loss exercise at some point. Someone interviews a dozen buyers, writes a deck, presents it to the leadership team, and the deck is filed. A year later the same losses are being explained in the same way.

The definition is settled and we will not repeat it here: What is win-loss analysis? covers what it is and how a first round works. This piece is about the harder part, which is keeping it running long enough to change decisions.

Why most programmes stop after one round

The one-off study fails for structural reasons rather than for lack of effort. Three are common.

It has no sampling rule. The first round interviews whoever will talk, which usually means friendly wins and a few dramatic losses. Nobody can say whether the findings describe the pipeline or the anecdotes.

It reports once. A single annual readout arrives months after the deals it describes, when the people involved have moved on. Clozd's own guidance is to deliver findings in small, regular doses rather than a year-end report, and to run collection continuously rather than in bursts.

It routes to nobody. The deck names themes ("pricing", "implementation concerns") but not owners. A theme with no owner is an observation, and observations do not get funded.

Gartner research summarised in trade press reports that organisations running rigorous, ongoing programmes see up to a 50% improvement in win rates; Clozd quotes the Gartner analyst Todd Berkowitz giving the same figure alongside a 15% to 30% increase in revenue. The baseline and method behind that figure are not published, so we treat it as direction. The direction matters: the benefit is attributed to the ongoing programme, not the study. Clozd's 2025 State of Win-Loss report, sponsored with The Alliance and drawing on more than 1,000 professionals, points the same way: 85% of ongoing, cross-functional programmes reported positive return on investment, against 55% of project-based ones, and 39% of companies said they ran an ongoing programme. Clozd sells win-loss services, so read both figures as vendor-reported.

What the evidence says about the reasons you already have

Every CRM holds a loss reason of some kind. The case for a programme rests on how often that field is wrong.

Clozd's figure of 15% alignment is the most quoted. A Showpad interview with Clozd's co-founder, published in August 2026, adds three more vendor-reported findings: about 85% of CRM loss reasons do not match what buyers say drove the decision; about 77% of the factors that influenced a decision never came up in sales conversations, based on comparing interviews with call recordings; and about 10% of closed-won customers were already at risk when interviewed, often because of implementation doubts.

The no-decision finding is the one most firms are not set up to capture. Matt Dixon and Ted McKenna's analysis of about 2.5 million recorded conversations, summarised by Challenger in 2024, found that 40% to 60% of lost deals ended with the buyer doing nothing. Their explanation is fear of making a mistake rather than preference for a rival. A CRM reason list that offers "lost to competitor" and "price" but not "no decision" will misclassify half the losses before anyone interviews anyone.

Evidence sourceWhat it gives youMain weaknessCost per deal
CRM loss reasonCoverage of every dealRecorded by the seller, often under time pressureNear zero
Call recordings and transcriptsWhat was said, verbatimMisses what the buyer never raised with youLow once recorded
Post-decision surveyScale and comparable scoresLow response; shallow answersLow
Buyer interviewThe buyer's actual reasoning, including internal politicsSlow; needs a skilled, neutral interviewerHighest

Forrester's 2025 best-practice report on win-loss treats surveys, interviews and call transcripts as complementary sources, and that is the right frame. The CRM field is the census. Interviews are the audit of the census. The design question is how to make the audit regular enough that the census improves.

A theme with no owner is an observation, and observations do not get funded.

Designing the programme

Five design choices decide whether a programme survives. Each has a sensible default that changes with size.

The sampling rule. Decide in advance which deals are eligible: by size, by segment and by outcome. Include no-decisions explicitly. Academic work on interview saturation points lower for a homogeneous group: Guest, Bunce and Johnson found the main themes in 60 interviews were present by about 12, and Hennink and colleagues found code saturation at nine interviews but that 16 to 24 were needed to understand the issues in depth. Clozd reports that thematic saturation tends to arrive at around 25 to 30 interviews per segment, which sets the ambition for a mid-size firm: one or two segments done properly beats six done thinly.

The interviewer. Buyers are more candid with someone who did not sell to them. Clozd's position, unsurprisingly for a third-party provider, is that sellers rarely get honest answers about their own losses. A smaller firm can use a senior person from outside the deal team, such as an operations lead or a partner from another practice. The rule is that the interviewer has no stake in the deal.

Timing. Interview within weeks of the decision, while the buyer still remembers the internal discussion. Enrol each eligible deal as it closes rather than batching at quarter end.

The coding frame. Fix a short list of themes before the first interview and code every answer against it. Add themes deliberately, with a date, rather than letting each analyst invent categories. Without a fixed frame, nobody can compare this quarter with last.

The readout cadence. Monthly to the revenue leader, quarterly to the leadership team. The monthly note is short: what came up, which themes are rising, which decisions are due for a check.

Design choiceAround 20 to 50 peopleAround 200 people
SampleEvery lost deal above a value threshold, plus every no-decisionRule by segment, with quotas per outcome
InterviewerSenior person outside the deal teamDedicated analyst or third party
VolumeTwo to four interviews a monthEnough to reach saturation per segment each half-year
Coding frameEight to ten themes on one pageVersioned frame owned by revenue operations
ReadoutMonthly note to the founder or revenue leadMonthly note plus quarterly review with product and finance
Where findings liveThe decision record, one line per themeThe decision record, linked to the deals that raised it

From finding to decision

The step most programmes skip is the one that matters: turning a coded theme into a decision someone owns.

Each recurring theme should produce one entry in the commercial decision record, using the same fields we set out in The commercial decisions worth recording: the decision, the reason, the owner, the status, the expected outcome with a check date, and the outcome written back.

Recurring themeNatural ownerTypical decisionWhat to check, and when
Buyers could not tell us apart from a rivalMarketing leadRewrite the positioning for one segmentWin rate against that rival, two quarters on
Deals stalled after the proposalRevenue leadAdd a risk-reduction step to the proposal standardNo-decision rate in that segment
Implementation worries late in the cycleDelivery leadIntroduce delivery staff before the final proposalLate-stage slippage and early churn
Price objections in one size bandFinance and revenueTest a package change in that bandDiscount depth and win rate in the band
Seller misread the buying groupSales managersChange qualification questionsStage conversion, next quarter

Two habits keep this honest. First, the record keeps the theme's evidence: how many interviews raised it, in which segment. Second, when a decision is revisited, it is superseded rather than edited, so the firm can later see what it believed and when, which is the argument of Supersede, never overwrite.

Feeding the census back

The programme should also improve the CRM field it audits. Once a quarter, compare the coded interview reason with the seller's recorded reason for the same deals. Where they disagree, ask whether the reason list is wrong or the recording habit is.

HubSpot's default deal properties, for example, include a separate closed-lost reason field with customisable options. Most CRMs offer an equivalent. The interview programme is how you decide what those options should be. What is a closed-lost reason? covers how to design a list people will fill in honestly. The minimum change is to add "no decision" as a reason in its own right, and to require a note when it is chosen.

Over time the gap between the census and the audit should narrow. If it does not, the problem is incentive rather than design. Sellers who expect a loss reason to be used against them will choose the least damaging option, and The reason nobody types explains why that pattern is predictable.

Where the programme sits in the commercial system

Win-loss is the point where the commercial system checks its own work. Qualification decides which deals to pursue. Discount governance decides what to concede. Proposals decide how to frame the offer. Forecasting decides what to expect. Win-loss is the only routine that asks the buyer which of those calls were right.

For the build order, that makes it the outcome half of the record. A qualification decision written down in March becomes evidence when a buyer explains in June why the deal went nowhere. Without the programme, the record holds decisions and outcomes but not causes, and a system trained on it can learn only correlation.

Illustrative example: one theme, one decision
Decision
Bring a delivery lead into every proposal meeting above a set deal value for two quarters.
Reason and owner
Six of the last nineteen interviewed losses in the mid-market segment named implementation risk as the deciding factor, and most were recorded in the CRM as price. Owned by the head of delivery, agreed with the revenue lead.
What changed
The proposal standard gained a delivery section; the no-decision rate in the segment is checked at the end of the second quarter.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size professional services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Run a programme, not a study. The benefit comes from ongoing collection and regular readouts, not one deck.
  • Sample by rule. Decide eligible deals in advance and include no-decisions explicitly.
  • Keep the interviewer neutral. Someone with no stake in the deal hears the real reason.
  • Route every theme to an owner. Each recurring finding becomes a recorded decision with a check date.
Gateway card

Before you call it a programme

  • A written sampling rule, including no-decision deals
  • An interviewer with no stake in the deals interviewed
  • A fixed coding frame of eight to ten themes
  • A monthly readout with a named recipient
  • Every recurring theme linked to one decision, one owner and one check date
  • "No decision" added to the CRM's loss reason list

Common questions

How many win-loss interviews do you need?

Enough to reach saturation in the segment you care about. Win-loss vendor Clozd reports that new themes tend to stop appearing at around 25 to 30 interviews per segment, so a mid-size firm should focus on one or two segments rather than spreading interviews thinly.

Should salespeople conduct win-loss interviews?

Generally not for their own deals. Buyers are more candid with someone who had no stake in the outcome, such as a senior colleague outside the deal team or a third party.

How soon after a deal closes should you interview the buyer?

Within weeks, while the buyer still remembers the internal discussion. Enrolling each eligible deal as it closes works better than batching at the end of a quarter.

What is the difference between win-loss analysis and a win-loss programme?

Analysis is the study of why deals were won or lost. A programme is the standing process around it: a sampling rule, regular interviews, a fixed coding frame, and a route from each finding to a decision someone owns.

Sources and notes

  • Hennink, Kaiser and Marconi, Code Saturation Versus Meaning Saturation: How Many Interviews Are Enough?, Qualitative Health Research, 2017. Peer-reviewed; health research interviews, not buyer interviews, and it also summarises Guest, Bunce and Johnson (Field Methods, 2006).
  • Clozd, Win-loss analysis guide. Vendor guide; source of the 15% alignment, participation and saturation figures. Methodology not published.
  • Gartner, Tech Go-to-Market: Three Ways Marketers Can Use Data From Win/Loss Analysis to Increase Win Rates and Revenues, as summarised in Business 2 Community via Yahoo News. Secondary summary; no date, sample or baseline given.
  • Clozd, 2025 State of Win-Loss Analysis Report, page updated August 2026. Vendor survey sponsored by Clozd and The Alliance; "more than 1,000 professionals", exact count and method not published; the page gives two different prior-year figures for ongoing programmes.
  • Clozd, Gartner report on the benefits of win-loss analysis. Vendor summary quoting Gartner's Todd Berkowitz; no Gartner report title or date given on the page.
  • Showpad, What buyer win-loss interviews reveal about the sales execution gap, August 2026. Vendor blog presenting Clozd's findings; interview counts not stated.
  • Challenger, How to Overcome Customer Indecision Using the JOLT Effect Approach, February 2024. Summary of Dixon and McKenna's research on about 2.5 million sales conversations.
  • Forrester, Uncovering The Reasons For Wins And Losses, July 2025. Analyst best-practice report; full text behind a paywall, only the summary was checked.
  • HubSpot Knowledge Base, HubSpot's default deal properties. Vendor documentation for the closed-lost reason field.
